newsitem.title: UK: Sterling/mark steady near highs, cable backtracks.
newsitem.headline: Sterling/mark steady near highs, cable backtracks.

text.p: 1130 GMT - Stg steadies below new 59-month high of 2.8880 marks set after UK data, amid corporate buying. Cable backtracks from intraday highs after stalling before $1.6725 resistance.
* Sterling/mark at 2.8860/70, up exactly a pfennig from late Thursday in Europe. Cable at $1.6666/78 vs $1.6660/65 yesterday.
* Final Q1 GDP up 3.1 pct y/y vs previous estimate of 3.0 pct. Q4 gain revised up to 1.1 pct in qtr from 0.8 pct. UK Q1 c/a surplus up to 1.459 bln stg vs 508 million in Q4 96.

* UK house prices rose 1.5 pct m/m, 11.0 pct y/y, Nationwide reports. Net mortgage lending up by 803 million stg in May, biggest increase since Jan, vs 751 million rise in April, BBA says. MIDDAY REPORT
Sterling leapt to a new 59-month high against the mark, reinvigorated by reports which underlined the need for higher UK interest rates and corporate buying.

Figures showed the British economy grew by 3.1 percent year-on-year in the first quarter, compared with an initial estimate of 3.0 percent, and there were upward revisions to growth figures from the past three years.
Reports from the British Bankers' Association and the Nationwide building society pointed to the strength of the housing market and also fanned expectations of higher rates.
"The numbers reiterated the arguments for sterling strength, and it looks like we will make an attempt on 2.90 before long," said Austin White, the foreign exchange manager at Yamaichi.

The pound was also boosted as UK corporates who had deferred selling foreign currency in the hope of getting better rates were forced to buy sterling with only one more trading day left before the end of the quarter, traders said.

Sterling rose as high as 2.8880 marks, the strongest it has been since July 1992. It was quoted at 2.8856/61 at 1005 GMT against 2.8753/58 late Thursday in Europe. Cable was at $1.6681/91 against $1.6660/65 yesterday.
Sterling has rallied 2.4 percent against the mark in the past week amid expectations UK domestic demand needs to be curbed if inflation is to remain in check.
Mounting evidence of the strength of consumer demand and the housing market has spurred traders to revise up expectations of how far rates will have to rise from their current 6.5 percent.

"The market is fairly well convinced that sterling can go higher because of the anticipated rate rises and the fact that the export market has not been hit as hard as people had expected by its rise," said Adam Cribben, the assistant chief trader at Credit Lyonnais.

Sterling has risen 20 percent since the beginning of August against a trade-weighted basket of 20 currencies. This has eroded UK exporters' competitiveness and the value of their foreign-currency earnings.

Still, a report Wednesday showed UK global exports rose 7.5 percent in April. Also, figures Friday showed the UK current account surplus grew to 1.459 billion pounds in the first quarter, almost three times expectations, from a 508 million pound surplus in the previous quarter.
Cribben at Credit Lyonnais also expects the pound to be bolstered by demand for UK assets.

Gilts offer a premium over their counterparts in most other European Union countries, and sterling is viewed by traders as a safe haven from concern that the planned European single currency will not be as strong as the mark, he said.
Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said Thursday there were signs that investors were transferring funds out of the mark into pounds, Swiss francs and dollars before EMU.
Sterling has cruised higher despite speculation that Chancellor Gordon Brown will tighten fiscal policy in his July 2 budget in a bid to curb runaway domestic demand.

A larger-than-expected tightening would deflate hopes of rate rises and risk weighing on the pound, analysts said. Traders, however, are betting that monetary policy will be left to do the bulk of the work in fighting inflation. -Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom, +44 171 542 6284
